subsystems.role: reaches and manipulates objects with human-like dexterity.

buildSteps.title: Set the kinematics
buildSteps.detail: Engineers choose the degrees of freedom, limb lengths and mass distribution so the robot can reach shelves, stairs and door handles, and calculate the joint torques needed.

buildSteps.title: Build joint actuators
buildSteps.detail: Each joint is a module: a brushless motor, a low-ratio or harmonic gearbox, an encoder and a torque sensor, tuned to be backdrivable so the limb gives way when pushed.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate hands
buildSteps.detail: Finger mechanisms are machined or moulded, tendons and return springs are threaded, and tactile pads are bonded onto the fingertips.

buildSteps.title: Assemble the body
buildSteps.detail: Frame, limbs and torso are bolted together, then hundreds of power and sensor cables are routed through the joints without failing as the joints rotate.

buildSteps.title: Integrate sensing and compute
buildSteps.detail: Cameras, IMU and tactile arrays are calibrated against each other; the onboard computer is mounted with cooling and connected to every actuator.

buildSteps.title: Train the control policy
buildSteps.detail: Most behaviour is learned first in physics simulation with randomised lighting, friction and payloads, then fine-tuned on real demonstrations, including teleoperated ones.

buildSteps.title: Test dexterity and endurance
buildSteps.detail: The robot runs repeated pick-place, stair and recovery trials while battery runtime and motor temperatures are logged.

buildSteps.title: Prove safety
buildSteps.detail: Force, pinch and collision tests are documented against human-robot safety standards before any deployment near untrained people.

buildSteps.title: Deploy and keep learning
buildSteps.detail: Fleets in pilot sites return data that improves the shared policy — this data loop, not any single breakthrough, is what would make the robot general.

prerequisites.why: vision-language-action models can map instructions and images to actions, but reliability on long, novel tasks is far below human level.
without high torque density in a light joint, a human-shaped limb cannot both move and lift.
lithium-ion packs give only a few hours of walking, so endurance limits useful work.
grasping unknown objects needs touch; vision-based and capacitive skin sensors exist but are not yet robust or cheap enough.
physics engines and domain randomisation make learning feasible, but contact-rich manipulation still transfers poorly.
existing rules cover fixed industrial and collaborative arms, not free-walking general-purpose androids working among people.

pathway.milestone: humanoids performing narrow, scripted tasks in warehouses and labs, often teleoperated
multi-task manipulation in structured settings without a human on the joystick
pathway.unlocks: commercially useful shifts in logistics and manufacturing.

pathway.milestone: language-directed general tasks plus certification for working beside people
pathway.unlocks: deployment in homes, hospitals and small businesses.

pathway.milestone: cheap mass-produced units with human-equivalent dexterity and reliability
pathway.unlocks: the labour-substitution and companionship uses people imagine today — the hardest part is reliability, not appearance.
